items.followUp: Define problem analysis and list two steps used to analyse a problem.

rubric.why: Shows that defining a problem means making its requirements and goal clear.
rubric.description: Defines problem definition as clearly stating the problem, its requirements, or its objective.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear definition containing the idea of stating what needs to be solved.

rubric.why: Identifying inputs and outputs establishes what information is available and what result is required.
rubric.description: Identifies the problem’s inputs and required outputs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark if both input and output are mentioned.

rubric.why: Constraints or limitations help determine what solutions are possible.
rubric.description: Mentions identifying constraints or limitations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant constraint or limitation.

rubric.why: Decomposition or abstraction is a strategy for making a problem easier to understand and define.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable strategy, such as breaking the problem into smaller parts or focusing on relevant details.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one relevant problem-defining strategy.

modelAnswer: Defining a problem means clearly stating what needs to be solved, its requirements and the result that is expected.
To define it, identify the available inputs, the required outputs and any constraints or limitations.
A useful strategy is to divide the problem into smaller sub-problems (decomposition).
Another strategy is abstraction: focus on the relevant details and ignore unnecessary information.

items.followUp: What is a computer network protocol? Name two protocols used on the Internet and state their functions.

rubric.why: A protocol suite is a collection of rules that enables devices to communicate.
rubric.description: Defines the TCP/IP suite as a set of communication protocols or rules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea of rules/protocols enabling communication.

rubric.why: TCP provides reliable delivery of data between devices.
rubric.description: Explains TCP as providing reliable data delivery.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for TCP and its reliable-delivery role.

rubric.why: IP addresses devices and routes packets between networks.
rubric.description: Explains IP as handling addressing or routing of packets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for IP and its addressing/routing role.

rubric.why: Application protocols provide familiar network services.
rubric.description: Names and correctly explains an application protocol, such as HTTP, FTP, SMTP or DNS.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct application protocol and its purpose.

modelAnswer: The TCP/IP suite is a set of protocols (rules) used for communication over the Internet and other networks.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides reliable delivery of data between devices.
IP (Internet Protocol) uses addresses and routes data packets to their destinations.
Application protocols include HTTP for web pages, FTP for file transfer, SMTP for sending email and DNS for translating domain names.

items.followUp: State two reasons for using passwords and list three features of a strong password.

rubric.why: The main purpose of a password is to prevent unauthorized access to an account or information.
rubric.description: States that passwords protect accounts, devices or data from unauthorized access.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the security purpose.

rubric.why: A longer password is generally harder to guess.
rubric.description: Mentions that a good password should be sufficiently long.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a length requirement or the idea that it should be long.

rubric.why: Using different character types makes a password harder to guess.
rubric.description: Recommends a mixture of character types, such as uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable combination of character types.

rubric.why: Avoiding predictable information and reused passwords improves security.
rubric.description: Advises avoiding easily guessed personal information or using a unique password.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one sensible security characteristic.

modelAnswer: A password protects an account, device or data from unauthorized access.
A good password should be long (preferably at least eight characters).
It should contain a mixture of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and special symbols.
It should be difficult to guess: avoid names and other personal information, and do not reuse it for different accounts.

items.followUp: Write the names of four common HTML elements and give one example of an HTML element.

rubric.why: These are names of common structural HTML elements.
rubric.description: Writes names of common structural elements such as html, head, title and body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least three correct structural element names.

rubric.why: These are names of common content or formatting HTML elements.
rubric.description: Writes names of common content elements such as h1, p, a, img, br, table or list elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least three correct content element names.

modelAnswer: Common HTML element names include html, head, title and body.
Other common elements include h1 (heading), p (paragraph), a (link), img (image) and br (line break).

items.followUp: Convert the hexadecimal number (3A)₁₆ to binary, showing the four-bit conversion for each digit.

rubric.why: Each hexadecimal digit corresponds to one group of four binary bits.
rubric.description: States the conversion method: replace each hexadecimal digit with its four-bit binary equivalent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct method.

rubric.why: The example confirms the method and gives the correct binary result.
rubric.description: Shows a correct conversion example or correct binary result.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example such as (2F)₁₆ = (00101111)₂.

modelAnswer: Replace each hexadecimal digit with its four-bit binary equivalent.
For example, (2F)₁₆ = 2 → 0010 and F → 1111.
Therefore, (2F)₁₆ = (00101111)₂.

items.followUp: Name four other examples of storage devices.

rubric.why: Hard disks and solid-state drives are common storage devices.
rubric.description: Names two valid storage devices.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

rubric.why: Flash drives, memory cards and optical discs are also storage devices.
rubric.description: Names two further valid storage devices.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two additional correct examples.

modelAnswer: Four examples of storage devices are a hard disk drive (HDD), a solid-state drive (SSD), a USB flash drive and a CD/DVD.

items.followUp: Use a truth table to verify the Boolean identity A·B = B·A.

rubric.why: The truth table must show the correct outputs for both expressions for all four input combinations.
rubric.description: Gives the correct truth-table values for A+B and B+A for all input combinations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a complete table with matching outputs in each row.

rubric.why: The matching columns verify the commutative law of Boolean OR.
rubric.description: States that the two expressions are equal and identifies or demonstrates the commutative law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equality or conclusion.

modelAnswer: The truth table is:
A | B | A+B | B+A
The columns for A+B and B+A are identical; therefore, A+B = B+A.
